title: Code Words for Resistance to Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Building on the prior day's discussion of Happy Talk, this article catalogs a series of common phrases that function as coded resistance to feedback, statements that sound reasonable on the surface but actually signal disagreement or refusal to change. Examples include "That doesn't match my experience" (code for disputing the data) and "No one else has ever said that to me" (code for rejecting the feedback outright). The author frames these phrases as a kind of resistance vocabulary that leaders need to learn to decode rather than take at face value. It closes by acknowledging that some pushback from confident high performers is natural, but insists leaders must push through the coded resistance to reach genuine agreement on next steps.
points: People resisting feedback often use coded phrases that sound cooperative but actually signal disagreement or rejection.
Examples like "I don't understand what you're telling me" or "You do the same thing" each carry an implicit, unstated counter-argument.
Good leaders learn to recognize these code phrases as a signal to check whether the feedback has actually landed.
Some resistance from confident, high-performing team members is natural, but leaders shouldn't let coded pushback substitute for real engagement and next steps.
quotes: People resist incorporating the feedback they receive by responding in ways that suggest they will make change when they really have no intention to do so.
That doesn’t match my experience." (Code for: Your data is wrong.)
No one else has ever said that to me.” (Code for: You are painfully wrong.)
Whenever a team member responds with any of the phrases above or those like them, the leader should explore whether their feedback has landed successfully.
Good leaders push through this shield of resistance and collaborate on a plan of action going forward.
